newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean Red Cross to resume food aid to North.
newsitem.headline: South Korean Red Cross to resume food aid to North.

text.p: The South Korean Red Cross on Monday said it would resume food shipments to North Korea this month for the first time since an incursion by a Northern submarine froze desperately-needed aid to the communist nation.
"We are shipping 300 tonnes of flour bought from donations by the Korean National Confederation of Churches," a Red Cross official said.
The announcement follows a Japanese news report that Washington is so worried North Korea is running out of food it is consulting Asian friends about an emergency rescue passage.
A North Korea expert in Tokyo said the United States may be deliberately spreading alarm to prepare the way for a large delivery of food to the North.

The timing of such a shipment would play into the hands of North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, and could give him the clout he needs to assume top party and government posts left unfilled since the death of his father Kim Il-sung, the expert added.
Speculation is rife that Kim Jong-il will be named General-Secretary of the Worker's Party and state president on the third anniversary of his father's death in July.
The South Korean Red Cross said 15,000 pairs of socks donated by groups in the country would be sent with the flour around January 25. The aid was worth $153,000.
All contacts with North Korea were halted after a North Korean Shark-class submarine dropped 26 armed intruders on a Southern beach on September 26.
Pyongyang issued a rare apology last month that satisfied Seoul, which returned the remains of 24 of the infiltrators who were shot and killed during a manhunt.

As part of a deal between Washington and Pyongyang that secured the apology, the United States agreed to ease a trade embargo on North Korea. U.S. grain giant Cargill Inc was granted permission to supply up to two million tonnes of grain to North Korea through barter trade.
Washington gave $2 million in February last year to alleviate hunger in North Korea caused by two consecutive years of devastating floods.
Japan's Kyodo News Service quoted an unnamed senior U.S. administration offical saying food stocks in North Korea could dry up almost completely in three to four months.

"We have to be thinking about the consequences for systemic failure in North Korea, both in terms of potential spillover in military forces, huge numbers of refugees, large humanitarian emergencies in terms of delivering foods and medicines," the official was quoted as saying.

U.S. and South Korean officials were scheduled to meet Pyongyang representatives in New York this month for preliminary discussions on proposed four-way talks, also including China, on a permanent peace to replace a truce accord that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
The North Korea expert in Japan said North Korea's Stalinist government could stagger on for five more years. Analysts in Seoul agreed that collapse was not imminent.

"We estimate that North Korea can maintain normal food distribution to its residents until the end of June," said an official at Seoul's Ministry of National Unification, who added that "normal" meant just enough to stave off hunger.
North Korea watcher Michael Breen said the Pyongyang government had a strategy for survival.

"North Korea will need to restart its rice diplomacy to obtain rice from Japan and South Korea. But it needn't be in a food crisis. The real problem is the structure of agriculture -- collective farming is inefficient," he said.
